objections.gloss: The objection equivocates on 'capacity.' The capacity valid consent requires has never meant emotional equanimity or the absence of distress; it is a decision-relative functional standard — the…
objections.title: A right to transition presupposes that the person validly consents to the interventions it covers, and valid consent requires decision-making capacity. But gender dysphoria is, by its own clinical description, a state of acute and sometimes severe psychological distress, and a person in the grip of such distress cannot weigh a decision of this magnitude soundly. Acute distress narrows attention, biases judgment toward relief, and impairs the dispassionate weighing of long-term consequences that competent consent demands — and the more the distress bears on the very thing being decided, the more it distorts the deciding, as a phobia distorts judgment of its object. So the consent on which the right rests is given from a state that defeats the capacity valid consent requires — and absent capacitated consent, there is no autonomous choice for the right to protect.

objections.gloss: The objection loses on the burden before any evidence is heard. A sex-role assigned at birth was assigned without the assignee's assent — and an ascription no one consented to cannot be the thing a…
objections.title: The burden is on the trans person to justify departing from their natal sex. Absent a successful justification — metaphysical (that one can change sex) or therapeutic (that intervention is medically necessary) — there is no right to transition; the default is to remain as assigned.

objections.gloss: Take the objection at its strongest, with outcome set aside: not that transition turns out badly, but that some changes admit no reversal — and that this alone forecloses the future self's option to…
objections.title: Set outcome entirely aside — grant that the chooser is glad of the change and never regrets it. The objection is that some of transition's bodily changes cannot be undone, and that this irreversibility is disqualifying in itself. An irreversible choice forecloses the future self's option to be otherwise, and that future person never consented to the foreclosure. A reversible choice leaves her free to revisit it; an irreversible one confiscates that freedom permanently. No one is entitled to foreclose another's options without consent, and the future self is, in the relevant sense, another — so the very permanence that makes the change momentous is what disqualifies it from the ordinary liberty to choose. The right must yield to the structure of the choice, whatever the present chooser feels about it.

objections.gloss: The objection equivocates on 'voluntary.' In consent doctrine voluntariness has never meant causally self-authored, or arising from a desire of asocial origin — it means free of coercion, duress, and…
objections.title: A right to transition presupposes that the person validly consents to acting on a desire to transition, and valid consent requires that the choice be voluntary. But the desire to transition is, in a growing number of cases, socially induced rather than the person's own: it spreads through peer clusters, online communities, and social media in patterns that look contagious — rapid, imitative, sharply clustered onset, often in cohorts with no prior history. A desire produced this way is not authentically the person's own; it is something caught from a social environment. Consent rooted in an induced desire is not voluntary in the sense valid consent requires, and an involuntary consent is no consent at all. So the right rests on a choice that is not, in these cases, freely the chooser's own — and absent a voluntary choice, there is no autonomous decision for the right to protect.

objections.gloss: The objection mislocates the decision. The harm it describes — regret, detransition, irreversible change — is self-regarding: it falls on the competent adult who chose to risk it, and the liberty to…
objections.title: A right to transition presupposes that the interventions it covers are the kind of thing a person may be left free to choose, and a choice that predictably ruins a substantial fraction of those who make it is not. Transition is such a choice. A significant share of those who transition come to regret it and detransition, often after changes that cannot be undone — sterility, surgically altered bodies, the lasting marks of cross-sex hormones — so that the regret, when it comes, falls on a person who can no longer return to what they were. This is not the ordinary risk attending any serious decision; it is grave, irreversible harm visited on the very people the right is meant to serve, at a rate no responsible practice would accept for an elective intervention. A liberty whose exercise inflicts harm of this severity on so many of those who exercise it does not earn protection as a right — the harm to the chooser is real enough, and common enough, to override the liberty interest, and the responsible course is to foreclose the option or hedge it with restrictions stringent enough that the harm is prevented rather than merely regretted.

objections.gloss: This objection differs from the others: it concedes the permission and points past it to a real third-party cost. Exercising the right — entering a sorted category, a changing room, a shelter, a…
objections.title: A right to transition does not stay self-regarding. Exercising it places trans women in sex-segregated sport, changing rooms, shelters, and prison wings, and that imposes real costs on cis women and girls who have competing claims of their own. The bodily advantages of a male-typical puberty — mass, skeletal frame, cardiovascular ceiling — are not erased by transition, making the female sports category unfair and, in contact sport, unsafe: cis competitors are displaced from podiums, records, and scholarships. And in single-sex provision for vulnerable women — domestic-violence shelters, women's prisons — inclusion can compromise privacy, dignity, or safety, against populations least able to absorb the cost. These are third parties with their own claims to fair competition, bodily privacy, and single-sex provision; the right reaches past the self and lands on them. A permission that harms others cannot be the modest, self-regarding thing it advertises.

objections.gloss: Defeating an objection to a right is not the same as recommending the act the right protects — they are distinct operations, and the suite performs only the first. To show that an objection fails to…
objections.title: The objection turns the suite's own Firewall against it. The charter forbids the suite from exhorting transition, from resting on a dysphoria-relief or any suffering-reduction premise, and from deploying a Benatar-style asymmetry. Yet a defense that systematically defeats every objection to transition cannot help but FUNCTION as advocacy: the cumulative brief makes the choice look unassailable, which is exhortation by other means. Worse, the defense must covertly rest on the merits it disclaims, for one defends a right to do X only because one judges X worth doing, so a suppressed dysphoria-relief premise is doing the real work; and the harm strand's signature move, concede the harm and defend the right to bear it, can only succeed if the foreclosure-harm silently outweighs the intervention-harm, a hidden asymmetry, a suffering-calculus in disguise. If any of this lands, the Firewall is a fiction, the expressivist and Benatar objections become true at the charter level, and the entire optionality framing is self-refuting.

objections.gloss: The objection assumes the only non-arbitrary stopping rule must rest on a metaphysical truth about which identity is real, so that severing gender self-ID from a truth-maker leaves bare…
objections.title: Once identity is severed from any external truth-maker and grounded in bare self-declaration, no non-arbitrary principle distinguishes the gender self-ID you protect from species, age, or race self-ID, which you do not. Either protect all of them — absurd, and corrosive of the categories and resources others rely on — or your protection of gender self-ID is arbitrary special-pleading. Any line you draw either re-imports the metaphysics you conceded or is bare stipulation. So self-ID grounds no right.

objections.gloss: The objection states the wing's own defense in its final line: a self-regarding permission cannot generate a duty in me. Just so — and it does not. The right is a liberty over one's own name, body…
objections.title: A right to transition does not stay in its lane. To recognize it is to conscript others into its upkeep: it requires me to speak words I hold false, to affirm in my professional capacity — as doctor, counselor, employer — an identity I reject, and to alter the records and language I am responsible for. My own liberties — speech, conscience, association, professional judgment — are self-regarding too, and this right tramples them. So it is not the modest self-regarding permission it advertises; it is a claim on my participation. And a self-regarding permission cannot generate a duty in me.

objections.gloss: The objection's force is in one inference: the body is a gift, so you owe the giver its preservation un-altered, and to alter it is ingratitude. Grant that the body is a gift — the inference still…
objections.title: Your body was given to you — by God, by nature, by your parents — as a gift. To alter it is ingratitude and defacement: you owe the giver the body's preservation, un-altered. Gender-affirming alteration breaks that debt of gratitude and disrespects the source of the gift, so you have no right to it.

objections.gloss: Concede the whole primitive, arguendo: sex is a biological fact, and ‘inner gender as essence’ names nothing coherent or falsifiable. The right is still untouched, because its objects were never an…
objections.title: No coherent referent grounds the gender you claim to self-determine. Sex is a biological fact, binary and immutable; an inner gender-as-essence is incoherent and unfalsifiable, tracking no fact of the matter. So self-determination has no object — nothing real is determined — and you assert a falsehood others are then asked to encode in speech and record.

objections.gloss: The objection equivocates on 'informed.' Valid informed consent has never required omniscient consent — knowledge of every long-term effect; it requires disclosure of the known material risks, honest…
objections.title: A right to transition presupposes that the person can give valid informed consent to the interventions it covers — cross-sex hormones, surgeries. Valid informed consent requires adequate information about consequences; but here the evidence base is thin and the long-term effects are genuinely uncertain — the durability of benefits, the rates and reversibility of harms, the effects on fertility, bone density, and cardiovascular and cognitive function over decades are not well established. A competent adult cannot give informed consent to interventions whose consequences are unknown: that is a leap in the dark dressed as autonomy, not informed consent. So the right rests on a consent that cannot in fact be given — and absent valid consent, there is no autonomous choice for the right to protect.
